Whatever is it that we are all looking for? I fancy that it is really quite close. When I was a boy I had a fancy that Heaven or Fairyland or whatever I called it, was immediately behind my own back, and that this was why I could never manage to see it, however often I twisted and turned to take it by surprise. I had a notion of a man perpetually spinning round on one foot like a teetotum in the effort to find that world behind his back which continually fled from him. Perhaps this is why the world goes round. Perhaps the world is always trying to look over its shoulder and catch up the world which always escapes it, yet without which it cannot be itself.

In any case, as I have said, I think that we must always conceive of that which is the goal of all our endeavours as something which is in some strange way near. Science boasts of the distance of its stars; of the terrific remoteness of the things of which it has to speak. But poetry and religion always insist upon the proximity, the almost menacing closeness of the things with which they are concerned. Always the Kingdom of Heaven is “At Hand”; and Looking-glass Land is only through the looking-glass. So I for one should never be astonished if the next twist of a street led me to the heart of that maze in which all the mystics are lost. I should not be at all surprised if I turned one corner in Fleet Street and saw a yet queerer-looking lamp; I should not be surprised if I turned a third corner and found myself in Elfland.

I should not be surprised at this; but I was surprised the other day at something more surprising. I took a turn out of Fleet Street and found myself in England.

.....

The singular shock experienced perhaps requires explanation. In the darkest or the most inadequate moments of England there is one thing that should always be remembered about the very nature of our country. It may be shortly stated by saying that England is not such a fool as it looks. The types of England, the externals of England, always misrepresent the country. England is an oligarchical country, and it prefers that its oligarchy should be inferior to itself.

message.content:
What is it that we are all in search of? I believe it is something remarkably close at hand. During my childhood, I envisioned a realm—be it Heaven or Fairyland—as existing just behind me, which is why I could never catch a glimpse of it, no matter how much I twisted and turned in an attempt to sneak up on it. I imagined a figure continuously spinning on one foot, like a top, trying to discover that elusive world that perpetually eluded him. Perhaps this notion explains the motion of the world; it is as if the world is forever attempting to glance over its shoulder in pursuit of the reality it cannot grasp, yet without which it cannot define itself.

Regardless, as I have mentioned, I maintain that the ultimate aim of our endeavors must be viewed as something curiously near. While science revels in the vast distances of its celestial bodies and the astonishing remoteness of its subjects, poetry and religion emphasize the immediacy, the almost threatening closeness of their themes. The Kingdom of Heaven is always described as “At Hand,” and the Land of Looking-glass exists merely through the looking-glass itself. Consequently, I would not be the least bit astonished if a sudden turn in the street led me straight to the core of that intricate maze where all mystics wander. I would not find it surprising if I turned a corner in Fleet Street and encountered a lamp of even stranger design; nor would it shock me if I rounded another corner and stumbled into Elfland.

While such surprises would not catch me off guard, I recently experienced something far more astonishing. Stepping off Fleet Street, I unexpectedly found myself in England.

The profound shock I felt might require some clarification. In the darkest or most challenging times within England, one essential truth about our nation should always be acknowledged. This can be succinctly expressed: England is not as foolish as it may appear. The various representations of England, the outward appearances, often mislead one’s understanding of the country. In reality, England operates as an oligarchy, deliberately choosing to present an oligarchic structure that is, in many ways, inferior to its true essence.
